message.content: Ich habe also vernommen — I have heard, then, that in Naukratis in Egypt there was one of the old gods there, to whom also the holy bird, which they indeed call Ibis, belonged; the demon himself, however, had the name Theuth. This one, it is said, first invented number and reckoning, and mathematics and star-knowledge, further board game and dice game, indeed even also the letters. Further, however, since at that time over all Egypt Thamus was king in the great city of the upper district, which the Hellenes call the Egyptian Thebes, as they call the god there Ammon, – so Theuth came to this one and showed him his arts and said that one must now communicate them to the other Egyptians. But he asked what kind of use each one had? As he now explained it, he knew, as it seemed to him that that one said something good or not good, to blame it now, to praise it now. Much, now, Thamus is said there to have said to Theuth about each art, in both directions, frankly, which to go through would require many words. But when he was at the letters, Theuth said: "This knowledge, O king, will make the Egyptians wiser and more capable of remembering; for as an aid for remembering as well as for wisdom it is invented." But he replied: "O you very artful[474] Theuth! Another is the one who, to bring forth what belongs to the art, another however the one who is able to judge what share of harm as well as of use it may bring to those who will use it. So have also you now, as father of the letters, out of fatherly love said the opposite of what their effect is. For forgetfulness this will bring about in the souls of those who get to know it, through neglect of remembering, inasmuch as they now, in trust in the writing, from outside by means of foreign signs, not from inside out of themselves, draw remembering. Not, then, for remembering, but for the memory have you invented an aid. Of wisdom, however, you offer the pupils only appearance, not truth. For many-hearers are they to you now without instruction, and so they will think themselves to be many-knowers, since they are yet commonly know-nothings and people with whom it is hard to get along, in that they have become seeming-wise, not wise."
message.reasoning:
I should translate this passage closely, keeping the literal sense of the German: the account of the old god at Naukratis in Egypt associated with the sacred bird they call Ibis, this deity's name being Theuth.

He was said to have first invented number and calculation, mathematics and astronomy, board games and dice, and even the letters themselves. Then I come to the part where Theuth, having these arts, approaches Thamus, the king ruling all of Egypt from the great city the Hellenes call Egyptian Thebes, to present his inventions and urge that they be shared with the other Egyptians.

I'm working through Thamus's response -- he questioned the usefulness of each art, and depending on whether Theuth's explanation seemed good or not, he would either praise or criticize it in turn.

When it came to writing specifically, Theuth claimed this invention would make the Egyptians wiser and better at remembering, serving as an aid to both memory and wisdom. But Thamus pushed back sharply, distinguishing between the one who invents an art and the one who can actually judge its benefits and harms to those who use it.

I'll settle on "Another is the one who, to bring forth what belongs to the art, another however the one who is able to judge."

Continuing: "So have also you now, as father of the letters, out of fatherly love said the opposite of what their effect is. For forgetfulness will this bring about in the souls of those who come to know it, through neglect of remembering, insofar as they now..."

I'm working through the next line: "...in trust in the writing, from outside by means of foreign signs, not from inside out of themselves, draw remembering." Then I'm checking "Not, then, for remembering, but for the memory have you invented an aid" -- weighing whether "Hilfsmittel" is best rendered as "aid" versus "auxiliary means," but "aid" keeps things consistent with earlier usage.

I'm continuing into Socrates's critique of Theuth's invention: that it offers pupils only the appearance of wisdom, not truth itself, since they'll hear much without real instruction and come to believe themselves knowledgeable when they're actually ignorant and difficult to deal with, having become merely seeming-wise rather than truly wise.
